title: Introductory Agrometeorology and Climate Change — Topic-Level Short Points
extraction_style: Deep extraction with short, separated points; semantic topic grouping; source terminology, formulas, classifications, numerical values, crop examples and procedures preserved; no page-by-page fragmentation.

chapters.title: Meaning and Scope of Agricultural Meteorology; Earth Atmosphere and Weather Variables

topics.title: Agricultural Meteorology
topics.definition: Applied meteorology dealing with crop and animal responses to the physical environment.

sections.heading: Meaning
content: Studies physical atmospheric processes producing weather in relation to agricultural production.
Includes meteorological, climatological and hydrological conditions significant to agriculture.
Focuses on interactions between environmental conditions and agricultural production.

sections.heading: Scope
content: Study climatic resources for effective production.
Quantify favourable weather normals for farm operations.
Develop crop/animal-weather relationships for productivity estimation.
Study weather–crop–pest and disease relationships.
Modify microclimate to increase agricultural productivity.
Delineate agro-ecological zones for efficient resource use and technology transfer.
Prepare crop-weather diagrams and crop-weather calendars.
Develop crop/animal growth simulation models.
Determine and monitor drought for drought management.
Provide value-added weather-based agro-advisories in real time.

topics.title: Weather and Climate
topics.definition: Weather is the short-term state of the atmosphere; climate describes longer-term average atmospheric conditions.

sections.heading: Weather
content: State of the atmosphere at a specific place and time.
Includes temperature, moisture, wind velocity and barometric pressure.
Usually concerns day-to-day changes over minutes to weeks.

sections.heading: Climate
content: Weather averaged over a long period and large area.
The source uses a 30-year period for climate normals.
Climate system components: atmosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere, land surface and biosphere.

sections.heading: Comparison
content: Weather is studied in meteorology.
Climate is studied in climatology.
Weather uses real-time atmospheric measurements.
Climate uses aggregated weather statistics over long periods.

topics.title: Weather Variables and Elements
topics.definition: The major weather elements used to describe weather and climate are temperature, pressure, wind, humidity and rain.

sections.heading: Major elements
content: Temperature indicates how hot or cold the atmosphere is.
Humidity is the amount of water vapour in the atmosphere.
Precipitation results from condensation processes and includes rain, snow, hail, sleet, drizzle, fog and mist.
Atmospheric pressure is the weight of air resting on the Earth's surface.
Wind is movement of air masses, especially near the Earth's surface.

sections.heading: Agricultural relevance
content: These elements provide the basis for weather forecasting.
Long-term analysis of the same elements supports climatology.

topics.title: Earth's Atmosphere: Composition
topics.definition: The atmosphere is a thick gaseous envelope surrounding Earth and held by gravitational force.

sections.heading: Gas composition
content: Nitrogen: 78.08% by volume.
Oxygen: 20.95%.
Argon: 0.93%.
Water vapour: 0–4% in the table.
Carbon dioxide: 0.0360% in the table.
Other trace gases include neon, helium, methane, hydrogen, nitrous oxide and ozone.
Nitrogen and oxygen together form about 99% of dry atmospheric volume.

sections.heading: Water vapour
content: Atmospheric vapour may range from zero to about 5% by volume in the text.
More than 90% of total atmospheric vapour occurs up to 5 km.
Water vapour absorbs terrestrial radiation and contributes to atmospheric heating.

sections.heading: Particulate matter
content: Includes dust, salt particles, pollen, smoke and volcanic ash.
Particles remain suspended in the atmosphere.
Selective scattering contributes to blue sky appearance.
Salt particles can act as hygroscopic nuclei for cloud and precipitation formation.

sections.heading: Ozone
content: Ozone is concentrated mainly around 15–55 km in the source discussion.
It absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation.
The source attributes severe ozone thinning primarily to chlorofluorocarbon emissions.

topics.title: Structure of Earth's Atmosphere
topics.definition: The atmosphere is divided into layers with characteristic temperature and physical properties.

sections.heading: Troposphere
content: Lowest atmospheric layer.
Average height about 12 km in one source description; 9 km at poles and 17 km at equator.
Contains roughly 75–80% of atmospheric mass.
Nearly all water vapour and dust occur here.
Most weather phenomena occur here.
Temperature normally decreases upward at about 6.5°C per km.
Upper boundary is the tropopause.

sections.heading: Stratosphere
content: Extends from roughly 12 km to 50–55 km.
Contains the ozone layer.
Temperature increases with altitude because ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation.
Atmosphere is stable with little weather-producing turbulence.
Upper boundary is the stratopause.

sections.heading: Mesosphere
content: Extends approximately from 50 km to 80–85 km.
Temperature decreases upward.
Most meteors burn up in this layer.
Mesopause is near 80–85 km and is the coldest atmospheric region in the source discussion.

sections.heading: Thermosphere and exosphere
content: Thermosphere begins near 80 km and temperature increases strongly with height.
Lower thermosphere contains the ionosphere.
Auroral phenomena occur in the thermosphere.
Exosphere is the outermost layer and merges into the solar wind.
Exosphere contains very low-density hydrogen and helium and many satellites.

topics.title: Agrometeorological Applications
topics.definition: Applications of atmospheric information for crop planning, productivity prediction and risk management.

sections.heading: Applications
content: Crop-weather calendars support timely farm operations.
Weather-crop relationships support productivity estimation.
Weather information helps manage drought.
Agro-ecological zoning supports resource-efficient production.
Growth simulation models can predict productivity and potential yield.
Weather-based advisories can reduce input costs and improve productivity.

topics.title: Atmospheric Pressure
topics.definition: Pressure exerted by the weight of air in the atmosphere.

sections.heading: Definition and variation
content: Low-pressure areas have less atmospheric mass above them.
High-pressure areas have more atmospheric mass above them.
Atmospheric pressure decreases with increasing elevation.
A one-square-centimetre column of air from sea level to the top of the atmosphere has a mass of about 1.03 kg.
Mean sea-level pressure is about 101.325 kPa = 1013.25 hPa = 1013.25 mbar.
Equivalent mean sea-level pressure is about 29.92 inHg or 760 mmHg.

sections.heading: Pressure and altitude
content: Increasing elevation reduces the mass of overlying air.
Mean sea-level pressure is the adjusted pressure commonly reported in weather reports.

topics.title: Wind and Forces Affecting Wind
topics.definition: Wind is air in motion caused primarily by spatial differences in atmospheric pressure.

sections.heading: Forces
content: Pressure-gradient force controls wind speed.
Pressure gradient is the rate of pressure change over space.
Coriolis force deflects medium- and large-scale air movement due to Earth's rotation.
Coriolis force depends on latitude and wind speed.
Centripetal force acts when wind follows curved paths around pressure centres.
Friction affects wind near the Earth's surface.

topics.title: Types of Wind
topics.definition: Winds are classified according to their scale, persistence and periodic behaviour.

sections.heading: Planetary winds
content: Blow throughout the year between latitude belts in response to pressure differences.
Major prevailing winds include trade winds and westerlies.

sections.heading: Trade winds
content: Blow from subtropical high-pressure belts near 30° toward the equatorial low-pressure belt.
Deflected right in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern Hemisphere.
Known as tropical easterlies.
Generally steady in direction and force.

sections.heading: Westerlies
content: Blow from subtropical high-pressure belts toward subpolar low-pressure belts.
Southern Hemisphere westerlies are described as stronger and more constant.
40°–65°S latitudes are associated with Roaring Forties, Furious Fifties and Shrieking Sixties.

sections.heading: Periodic winds
content: Direction changes periodically with seasons or daily heating differences.
Examples: monsoons, land/sea breezes, mountain/valley breezes.

sections.heading: Local winds
content: Produced by local temperature and pressure differences.
Types listed: hot, cold, convectional and slope winds.

topics.title: Land and Sea Breezes
topics.definition: Local coastal winds produced by differential heating and cooling of land and water.

sections.heading: Land breeze
content: Occurs mainly at night.
Land cools faster than the sea.
Air flows from relatively higher-pressure land toward lower-pressure water.
Usually weaker than the daytime sea breeze.
Dies as land warms the next morning.

sections.heading: Sea breeze
content: Develops after sunrise as land heats faster than water.
Warm air over land expands and lowers surface pressure.
Air moves from relatively higher-pressure sea toward lower-pressure land.
Strength increases with the land–sea temperature difference.
A strong offshore wind above about 15 km/h can prevent development.

topics.title: Mountain and Valley Breezes
topics.definition: Diurnal mountain winds caused by differential heating and cooling of mountain slopes and valleys.

sections.heading: Valley breeze
content: Occurs during the day.
Heated mountain slopes cause air to move upward from valleys.

sections.heading: Mountain breeze
content: Occurs after sunset.
Cold dense air moves downslope from mountains toward valleys.

topics.title: Cyclones and Anticyclones
topics.definition: Cyclones are low-pressure systems with inward rising flow; anticyclones are high-pressure systems with outward surface flow and subsidence.

sections.heading: Cyclone
content: Large-scale air mass rotating around a strong low-pressure centre.
Northern Hemisphere rotation is counter-clockwise.
Southern Hemisphere rotation is clockwise.
Surface air converges inward and rises near the centre.
Rising air expands and cools, increasing humidity and cloudiness.
Cyclones are generally associated with rain, clouds and unsettled weather.

sections.heading: Tropical cyclone
content: Warm-core system driven by significant convective activity and latent heat release.

Six source-listed requirements: warm sea surface, atmospheric instability, lower/middle tropospheric humidity, sufficient Coriolis force, pre-existing low-level disturbance, and low vertical wind shear.
Called hurricane in the Atlantic/northeastern Pacific.
Called cyclone in the Indian and South Pacific oceans.
Called typhoon in the northwestern Pacific.

sections.heading: Extratropical cyclone
content: Also called mid-latitude or wave cyclone.
Large-scale low-pressure system generally occurring in middle latitudes.
Often develops along strong temperature/dew-point gradients and fronts.
Associated with significant vertical wind shear and jet-stream dynamics.
Usually occurs between about 30° and 60° latitude.
Can produce cloudiness, showers, gales and thunderstorms.
Often develops through frontal waves and later occludes.

sections.heading: Anticyclone
content: High-pressure system.
Northern Hemisphere winds rotate clockwise.
Southern Hemisphere winds rotate counter-clockwise.
Air descends and warms by compression.
Subsidence reduces humidity and cloud formation.
Generally associated with clear skies and light surface winds.

topics.title: Solar Radiation
topics.definition: Radiant energy emitted by the Sun and the prime external energy source for Earth's biosphere.

sections.heading: Sun and energy
content: Solar radiation is the flux of radiant energy from the Sun.
Sun diameter: about 1.39 × 10^6 km.
Mean Sun–Earth distance: about 1.5 × 10^8 km.
Source gives solar surface temperature around 5462 K in one description.
Energy is produced by fusion in which hydrogen is transformed to helium.
The source states about 99% of biosphere energy comes from the Sun.

sections.heading: Insolation
content: Electromagnetic energy radiated into space by the Sun.
Factors affecting insolation: solar constant, atmospheric transparency, duration of daily sunlight and noon solar angle.

topics.title: Heat Transfer Processes
topics.definition: Heat moves by conduction, convection and radiation.

sections.heading: Conduction
content: Heat transfer through matter without bulk movement of the substance.
Heat flows from warmer to cooler parts.
Example: heating along an iron rod.

sections.heading: Convection
content: Heat transfer through actual movement of molecules or fluid masses.
Predominant in many atmospheric weather processes.
Example: boiling water.

sections.heading: Radiation
content: Energy transfer by electromagnetic waves without a material medium.
Solar energy reaches Earth by radiation.
Radiation produces heat when absorbed by a surface.

topics.title: Solar Spectrum and Wavelength Bands
topics.definition: Solar radiation spans a broad electromagnetic spectrum with different wavelengths and biological effects.

sections.heading: Major bands
content: Ultraviolet: about 0.20–0.39 μm.
Visible radiation: about 0.39–0.76 μm.
Infrared: greater than 0.76 μm in the source table.
Visible colours progress from violet through indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange and red.

sections.heading: Plant significance
content: Visible light is essential for photosynthesis.
Infrared provides thermal energy.
Shorter-than-visible radiation is chemically active and potentially damaging.
Ultraviolet radiation is strongly absorbed by atmospheric ozone.

sections.heading: Wavelength units
content: 1 millimicron = 10^-9 m = 10^-7 cm.

topics.title: Solar Radiation and Crop Plants
topics.definition: Crop production depends on the intensity, quality and duration of solar radiation.

sections.heading: Spectral effects
content: Radiation below visible wavelengths can be detrimental at high exposure.
Infrared has a thermal effect and supplies thermal energy to the plant environment.
Visible light is indispensable to photosynthesis.
Light affects tillering, culm stability, culm length, yield, plant biomass, leaf size and root development.

sections.heading: Critical stages
content: Maize: radiation intensity during the third month is highlighted.
Rice: about 25 days before flowering.
Barley: flowering period.

sections.heading: Specific spectral bands
content: 700–900 nm far-red region influences photoperiodism, germination, flowering and fruit coloration.
720–510 nm is strongly absorbed by chlorophyll and has strong photosynthetic activity.
510–400 nm includes strong chlorophyll/yellow pigment absorption and strong blue-violet photosynthetic effects.
400–315 nm can produce formative and dwarfing effects.
Below 280 nm has lethal/germicidal effects in the source.

topics.title: Radiation Balance, Albedo and Earth Energy Budget
topics.definition: Radiation balance is the difference between incoming and outgoing radiation; albedo is the percentage of incident radiation reflected by a surface.

sections.heading: Radiation properties
content: Absorptivity = absorbed radiant energy / incident radiant energy.
Reflectivity = reflected radiant energy / incident radiant energy.
Albedo is reflectivity expressed as a percentage.
Transmittivity = transmitted radiation / incident radiation.
Emissivity = radiation emitted by a surface / radiation emitted by a blackbody under comparable conditions.
A blackbody completely absorbs incident radiation and has absorptivity and emissivity of unity.

sections.heading: Earth energy budget
content: The atmosphere filters, absorbs, scatters and reflects solar radiation.
Source example: 324 W m^-2 reaching Earth in the upper-atmosphere budget discussion.
236 W m^-2 are re-emitted to space as infrared radiation in the cited budget.
86 W m^-2 are reflected by clouds.
20 W m^-2 are reflected by the ground as short-wave radiation.
Atmospheric absorption and re-radiation contribute to the greenhouse effect.

sections.heading: Albedo values
content: Pure water: 5–20%.
Vegetation: 10–40%.
Clouds: about 55%.
High albedo means more incident solar radiation is reflected.
Albedo depends on incidence angle, surface properties, season and time of day.
Crop-community albedo depends on crop age, ground cover, foliage colour and reflectivity.

topics.title: Outgoing Long-Wave Radiation
topics.definition: Long-wave radiation emitted by the heated Earth and modified by atmospheric absorbers.

sections.heading: Characteristics
content: Average Earth surface temperature is given as about 285 K in the source.
About 99% of emitted terrestrial radiation is in the infrared range of 4–120 μm.
About 90% of outgoing radiation is absorbed by the atmosphere in the source discussion.
Water vapour absorbs in approximately 5.3–7.7 μm and beyond 20 μm.
Ozone absorbs around 9.4–9.8 μm.
CO2 absorbs around 13.1–16.9 μm.
Clouds absorb across broad wavelengths.

sections.heading: Atmospheric window
content: Long-wave radiation escapes relatively freely between about 8.5 and 11 μm.
This region is called the atmospheric window.
The source notes its use in microwave remote sensing and its role in limiting excessive night cooling through counter-radiation.

topics.title: Radiation Laws
topics.definition: Physical relationships connecting wavelength, frequency, energy, emission and temperature.

sections.heading: Wave relation
content: λ = c/ν.
λ = wavelength.
c = velocity of light ≈ 3 × 10^10 cm s^-1.
ν = frequency.

sections.heading: Planck's law
content: E = hν.
h = Planck's constant ≈ 6.62 × 10^-34 J s.
Higher frequency means higher quantum energy.
Shorter wavelength corresponds to higher frequency and energy.

sections.heading: Kirchhoff's law
content: a(λ) = e(λ).
A good absorber is a good emitter under similar conditions.

sections.heading: Stefan–Boltzmann law
content: E = σT^4.
T is absolute temperature in kelvin.
σ ≈ 5.673 × 10^-8 W m^-2 K^-4 for the blackbody constant given.

sections.heading: Wien's displacement law
content: λmax = 2897/T μm.
Higher temperature shifts maximum emission toward shorter wavelengths.
For Sun temperature around 5793 K, λmax is about 0.5 μm.
For Earth surface near 287 K, λmax is about 10 μm.

topics.title: Air Temperature and Temperature Factors
topics.definition: Air temperature describes the molecular kinetic state of air and strongly controls atmospheric and crop processes.

sections.heading: Definition and heat transfer
content: Temperature is described as a measure of molecular motion.
Heat is energy associated with molecular motion and transfer due to temperature differences.
Conduction, convection and radiation transfer heat.

sections.heading: Factors affecting air temperature
content: Latitude.
Altitude.
Distribution of land and water.
Ocean currents.
Prevailing winds.
Cloudiness.
Mountain barriers.
Nature of surface and relief.
Convection and turbulence.

sections.heading: Examples
content: Northern India source example: January is the coldest month and June the warmest.
Southern India source example: December is the coldest month and May the warmest.
Land shows larger temperature variations than water.
Ocean currents redistribute heat and create temperature contrasts.

topics.title: Diurnal and Seasonal Temperature Variation
topics.definition: Air temperature changes systematically within a day and across seasons.

sections.heading: Diurnal variation
content: Minimum air temperature generally occurs near sunrise.
Temperature rises after sunrise and reaches a maximum around 13:00–14:00 h.
Temperature then declines toward sunrise.
Difference between daily maximum and minimum is the diurnal range.
Clear days have larger diurnal ranges.
Cloudy conditions reduce daily temperature amplitude.
Daily mean temperature = (daily maximum + daily minimum) / 2.

sections.heading: Seasonal variation
content: Northern Hemisphere winter minimum is stated as January.
Northern Hemisphere summer maximum is stated as July.

sections.heading: Horizontal distribution
content: Isotherms join places with equal temperature.
Temperature generally decreases from equator toward poles.
Land-water distribution modifies latitudinal temperature patterns.
Mountain barriers and local topography alter horizontal temperature distribution.

topics.title: Vertical Temperature Distribution
topics.definition: Atmospheric layers can be distinguished by how temperature changes with altitude.

sections.heading: Troposphere
content: Average height about 14 km in this chapter; about 16 km at equator and 7–8 km at poles.
Seat of weather phenomena.
Temperature decreases upward at about 6.5°C/km.
Contains most atmospheric moisture and aerosols.

sections.heading: Stratosphere
content: Extends roughly from 20 km to 50–55 km in the source chapter.
Called a seat of photochemical reactions.
Temperature increases with height.
Ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation and warms the upper stratosphere.
Upper boundary is the stratopause.

sections.heading: Mesosphere and ozonosphere
content: Ozone concentration is highlighted between about 30 and 60 km.
Ozone absorbs UV radiation.
Mesosphere lies approximately 50–80 km.
Mesospheric temperature decreases with height.
Mesopause temperature may reach nearly −95°C in the source.

sections.heading: Thermosphere and exosphere
content: Thermosphere/ionosphere extends from about 80 km to 400 km in the chapter.
Temperature rises again and may reach about 1000°C.
Ionosphere reflects radio waves and supports long-distance radio communication.
Exosphere is the outermost layer, roughly 400–1000 km in this chapter.
Hydrogen and helium predominate in the exosphere.

topics.title: Lapse Rate and Adiabatic Processes
topics.definition: Lapse rate is temperature change with height; adiabatic temperature change occurs without external heat exchange.

sections.heading: Lapse rates
content: Average atmospheric lapse rate is about 6.5°C/km.
Dry adiabatic lapse rate is about 10°C/km.
Moist adiabatic lapse rate is usually below 6°C/km.
Moist air cools more slowly because condensation releases latent heat.

sections.heading: Mountain process
content: Moist air forced upward over mountains expands and cools.
Cooling may cause condensation and precipitation.
Descending air becomes warmer and drier after losing moisture.
Descending air warms at the dry adiabatic rate in the source explanation.

sections.heading: Adiabatic change
content: No outside heat is involved.
Rising air expands and cools.
Sinking air compresses and warms.

topics.title: Temperature Inversion
topics.definition: A temperature inversion occurs when temperature increases with altitude over a layer instead of decreasing normally.

sections.heading: Causes
content: Ground air can cool faster than overlying air during clear cooling nights.
A warm layer may pass over a lower cold layer.
Cold air can drain downslope and be replaced by warmer air.

sections.heading: Significance
content: Influences cloud formation and precipitation.
Can cause fog near the ground.
Reduces visibility and can affect air navigation.
Affects diurnal temperature behaviour and conversion of incoming solar radiation to heat.

topics.title: Heat Units and Growing Degree Days
topics.definition: Heat units quantify accumulated warmth above a crop-specific threshold during growth.

sections.heading: GDD concept
content: Heat unit represents departure of mean daily temperature above a minimum threshold.
Base temperatures in the source commonly range from 4.5–12.5°C.
6.0°C is stated as a commonly used value.

sections.heading: Formula
content: GDD = Σ[(Tmax + Tmin)/2 − Tb].
Tmax = daily maximum air temperature.
Tmin = daily minimum air temperature.
Tb = crop base or threshold temperature.

sections.heading: Uses
content: Guide agricultural operations and planting land use.
Forecast crop harvest dates, yield and quality.
Estimate labour requirements.
Support introduction of crops and varieties into new areas.
Predict likelihood of successful crop growth.

topics.title: Heat and Cold Injuries in Crops
topics.definition: Extreme temperatures cause physiological and physical injuries to crop plants.

sections.heading: Heat injury
content: Thermal death point is given as about 50–60°C, varying with species.
Aquatic and shade-loving plants may be killed at around 40°C.
High temperature causes desiccation.
It disrupts photosynthesis and respiration.
High temperature increases respiration and rapidly depletes stored food.

sections.heading: Cold injury
content: Chilling injury affects warm-climate plants exposed to low temperatures.
Sugarcane, sorghum and maize may show chlorotic bands when night temperature falls below 20°C in the source example.
Freezing injury forms ice crystals in plant tissues and dehydrates cells.
Examples include frost damage in potato and tea.
Suffocation can occur under thick ice/snow due to restricted oxygen entry.
Heaving occurs when ice crystals expand soil and mechanically lift plants.

sections.heading: Specific injury
content: Stem griddle is bark/stem injury associated with high daytime and low nighttime temperatures.
Young cotton seedlings in sandy soil may be affected when soil temperature exceeds 60°C.

topics.title: Role of Temperature in Crop Production
topics.definition: Temperature controls crop distribution, development, physiological processes and productivity.

sections.heading: Crop effects
content: Influences crop and vegetation distribution.
Affects leaf production, expansion and flowering.
Changes gas and liquid diffusion rates.
Affects solubility of substances.
Biochemical reaction rates increase strongly with temperature; the source states reactions may double or more per 10°C rise.
Affects enzyme stability and system equilibrium.
Most higher plants grow between about 0–60°C; crop plants are more restricted, around 10–40°C.
Maximum dry matter production is stated around 20–30°C.
High temperature plus high humidity favours some pests and diseases.
High night temperature increases respiration and metabolism.

sections.heading: Cardinal temperatures
content: Crops have minimum, optimum and maximum temperatures.
Wheat and barley: minimum 0–5°C; optimum 25–31°C; maximum 31–37°C.
Sorghum: minimum 15–18°C; optimum 31–36°C; maximum 40–42°C.

sections.heading: Thermoperiodism
content: Response of living organisms to regular temperature changes between day and night or seasons.

topics.title: Soil Temperature
topics.definition: Soil temperature influences seed, root and microbial processes and is controlled by meteorological and soil factors.

sections.heading: Importance
content: Governs uptake of water and nutrients.
Controls soil microbial activity; source optimum range is 18–30°C.
Influences seed germination and root development.
Influences mineralization of organic nitrogen.
Low soil temperature favours greater persistence of organic matter.
Affects mineral weathering and soil reactions.
Influences soil structure and exchangeable ions.

sections.heading: Meteorological factors
content: Solar radiation directly affects soil temperature.
Wind/convection transfers heat to the soil.
Evaporation cools soil.
Condensation and freezing can release heat.
Precipitation may warm or cool soil depending on its temperature.

sections.heading: Soil factors
content: Slope/aspect affect received insolation.
Sandy soils warm faster than clay soils.
Light soils generally show larger temperature ranges.
Tillage and soil mulch modify heat flow and moisture.
Organic matter lowers heat capacity and thermal conductivity while increasing water-holding capacity.
Dark soils absorb more radiation than light soils.
Moisture increases heat capacity and conductivity and cools the surface through evaporation.

sections.heading: Daily and seasonal variation
content: At 5 cm depth, daily change can exceed 10°C.
At 20 cm the daily change is smaller.
At about 80 cm, diurnal changes are practically nil.
Heat penetrates downward with a time lag.
Seasonal variations penetrate deeper than diurnal variations.
Plant canopy reduces seasonal soil-temperature variation.

topics.title: Atmospheric Humidity
topics.definition: Humidity is the amount of water vapour present in air.

sections.heading: Meaning and sources
content: Humidity is a highly variable climatic factor.
Source gives atmospheric water vapour as roughly 0–4% by volume, averaging around 2%.
Measured with a hygrometer.
Water vapour enters the atmosphere through evaporation, plant transpiration and animal respiration.

sections.heading: Importance
content: Supports precipitation formation.
Absorbs incoming and terrestrial radiation and influences Earth's heat budget.
Stores latent energy important in storms and cyclones.
Influences sensible temperature and human cooling.

topics.title: Absolute Humidity
topics.definition: Weight of actual water vapour present per unit volume of air.

sections.heading: Definition
content: Usually expressed as grams of water vapour per cubic metre of air.
Warm air can hold more water vapour than cold air.
At 10°C, one cubic metre of air can hold about 11.4 g water vapour in the source example.
At 21°C, the same volume can hold about 22.2 g.

sections.heading: Limitation
content: Not a fully reliable index because temperature and pressure change air volume and therefore absolute humidity.

topics.title: Relative Humidity and Saturation
topics.definition: Relative humidity is the ratio of actual water vapour content to the moisture-holding capacity of air at a given temperature, expressed as a percentage.

sections.heading: Relative humidity
content: Adding moisture by evaporation increases relative humidity.
Cooling air decreases its moisture-holding capacity and increases relative humidity.
Saturated air has relative humidity of 100%.
Air containing half of its moisture-holding capacity has relative humidity of 50%.
Relative humidity strongly influences evaporation.

sections.heading: Dew point
content: Temperature at which a given air sample becomes saturated without changing its moisture content.
Further cooling below the dew point promotes condensation.

topics.title: Specific Humidity and Mixing Ratio
topics.definition: Specific humidity relates water-vapour mass to total moist-air mass; mixing ratio relates water-vapour mass to dry-air mass.

sections.heading: Specific humidity
content: Weight of water vapour per unit weight of air.
Usually expressed in grams per kilogram.
Less affected by changes in pressure or temperature than absolute humidity.

sections.heading: Mixing ratio
content: Mass of water vapour divided by mass of dry air.
Expressed as grams of water vapour per kilogram of dry air.

topics.title: Saturation and Vapour Pressure
topics.definition: Saturation occurs when evaporation and condensation reach dynamic equilibrium at a given temperature.

sections.heading: Saturation
content: Saturation does not mean evaporation stops.
In a closed water system, evaporation initially exceeds condensation.
At equilibrium, evaporation rate equals condensation rate and the air is saturated.
Higher temperature permits more water to remain in the vapour phase.

sections.heading: Vapour pressure
content: Saturation vapour pressure increases with air temperature.
Below 0°C, saturation curves differ over liquid water and ice.
Supercooled liquid water can persist below 0°C in clouds.

sections.heading: Vapour pressure deficit
content: VPD = saturated vapour pressure (SVP) − actual vapour pressure (AVP).
VPD is useful in crop-growth and atmospheric-moisture studies.

topics.title: Condensation
topics.definition: Condensation is the change of water vapour into liquid or solid form when atmospheric conditions exceed moisture-holding capacity.

sections.heading: Requirements
content: Cooling moist air can reduce moisture-holding capacity below actual vapour content.
Condensation generally begins when air temperature reaches or falls below the dew point.
Relative humidity near 100% means the air is near saturation.
Dust, smoke, pollen and ocean salt can act as hygroscopic condensation nuclei.

sections.heading: Ways condensation can occur
content: Air temperature can fall to the dew point at approximately constant volume.
Air volume can increase without addition of heat.
Combined temperature and volume changes can reduce moisture-holding capacity.
Evaporation can add moisture to the air.

sections.heading: Products
content: Condensation may produce dew, frost, fog, mist and clouds.
Direct vapour-to-solid deposition is described as sublimation in the source.

topics.title: Adiabatic and Non-Adiabatic Cooling
topics.definition: Cooling processes that produce condensation are classified into adiabatic and non-adiabatic changes.

sections.heading: Adiabatic cooling
content: Rising air expands and cools without external heat loss.
Vertical air displacement is a major cause of adiabatic temperature change.
Katabatic flow is cold, dense air moving downslope.

sections.heading: Non-adiabatic cooling
content: Includes cooling by radiation, conduction or mixing with colder air.
Radiational cooling can produce fog or clouds when nuclei are present.
Contact cooling can produce dew, frost or fog.
Effects are mainly confined to a thin atmospheric layer.
Source states non-adiabatic cooling generally produces dew, fog or frost rather than substantial precipitation.

topics.title: Dew, Frost, Fog, Mist, Haze and Smog
topics.definition: These are near-surface atmospheric moisture or particulate phenomena formed under different temperature, humidity and condensation conditions.

sections.heading: Dew
content: Water droplets deposited on cool solid surfaces such as leaves, grass and stones.
Ideal conditions: clear sky, calm air, high relative humidity, cold and long nights.
Dew point must be above freezing.

sections.heading: White frost
content: Forms on cold surfaces when condensation occurs at or below 0°C.
Moisture deposits as minute ice crystals rather than liquid droplets.
Formation conditions resemble dew except temperature is at or below freezing.

sections.heading: Fog
content: Cloud with base at or very near the ground.
Visibility is less than 1 km in the source.
Radiation fog forms from radiational cooling and is common in winter.
Advection fog forms when warm air moves over a cold surface; it is thick and persistent.
Frontal or precipitation fog forms near converging warm and cold air masses.

sections.heading: Mist
content: Contains more moisture per nucleus than fog in the source description.
Droplets are less coalesced, so mist is less dense and dissipates faster.
Visibility is more than 1 km but less than 2 km.

sections.heading: Haze and smog
content: Haze occurs when dust, smoke and dry particles reduce sky clarity without condensation.
Sources include farming in dry weather, traffic, industry and wildfires.
Smog = smoke + fog.
Source links smog to coal burning, vehicle emissions and industrial fumes.

topics.title: Importance and Variation of Humidity for Crops
topics.definition: Atmospheric humidity interacts with temperature, rainfall and wind to influence crop water relations, pests, diseases and yield.

sections.heading: Crop effects
content: Helps determine which crops can be grown in a region.
Affects internal plant water potential.
Influences transpiration and potential evapotranspiration.
Determines crop water requirement.
High humidity can reduce irrigation requirement by reducing evapotranspiration losses.
High humidity can prolong crop survival under moisture stress.
Very high or very low relative humidity is generally unfavorable for high yields in the source.
High humidity favours some fungi, bacteria and pests.
Examples include potato blight and thrips/jassid damage.
High humidity during grain filling can reduce yield.
Very high relative humidity is described as beneficial to maize, sorghum and sugarcane but harmful to sunflower and tobacco.
Moderate relative humidity above 40% is described as generally safe for most crops.

sections.heading: Variation
content: Absolute humidity is highest near the equator and lowest near the poles.
Absolute humidity is minimum around sunrise and maximum around 14:00–15:00 in the source.
Relative humidity is generally maximum near sunrise and minimum around 14:00–15:00.
The source gives relative humidity around 80% at the equator and around 85% at the poles, with about 70% near horse latitudes.

topics.title: Climatic Normal
topics.definition: A climatic normal is the average value of a weather element over 30 years.

sections.heading: Meaning and use
content: The period may be represented by weekly, monthly or annual averages.
Crop distribution, production and productivity depend on climatic normals.
Crop selection based on optimum climatic requirements can improve production potential.

topics.title: Weather Forecasting
topics.definition: Prediction of weather from the next few hours to seasonal periods.

sections.heading: Importance for agriculture
content: Weather has major social and economic impacts.
The source states weather aberrations alone can explain up to 50% variation in crop production.
Rainfall is especially important for crop production and regional economy.
Forecasts support moisture conservation during weak monsoon conditions.
Forecasts support flood-relief planning during strong monsoon conditions.
Timely pest and disease warnings can reduce recurring crop losses.
Forecasts help plan water use.
Reliable forecasts can support sustainability and reduce damage from adverse weather.

sections.heading: Forecast types
content: Nowcast: next few hours.
Short-range: about 24 hours, with outlook for another 24 hours.
Medium-range: about 3–7/10 days.
Long-range: beyond 7 days up to a season.
Seasonal climate forecast supports farm decisions, especially rainfall-related decisions.

topics.title: Forecast Services, Users and Accuracy
topics.definition: Forecast services differ in lead time, predicted elements, methods and agricultural users.

sections.heading: Service table
content: Nowcasting: IMD; thunderstorms, dust storms, cold/heat waves; lead time 1–2 hours; source accuracy 90–98%.
Short range: IMD; cloud spread, rainfall, temperature and cyclone warnings; lead time about 1 day; source accuracy 80–90%.
Medium range: IMD; rainfall, temperature, relative humidity, wind speed/direction and cloud cover; 3–10 days; source accuracy 70–75%.
Long range: IMD; seasonal rainfall; 30–40 days in the source table; source accuracy about 60%.

sections.heading: Methods
content: Synoptic method uses surface and upper-air observations from multiple locations and prepares charts of atmospheric status.
Statistical methods include multiple regression and ARIMA.
Numerical weather prediction integrates equations representing Coriolis, frictional, pressure-gradient and gravitational forces.
NWP model results depend strongly on accurate initial conditions.

sections.heading: Farmer use
content: Forecasters should understand crops grown in each agroclimatic zone.
Forecast warnings should match crop growth stages.
Farmers need to understand and interpret weather bulletins.

topics.title: Climate Change and Global Warming
topics.definition: Climate change is a significant long-term change in expected regional or global weather patterns; accelerated change is linked in the source to anthropogenic activities and greenhouse gases.

sections.heading: Climate change
content: Can occur over decades, centuries or much longer periods.
The source emphasizes faster recent change associated with industrialization, urbanization, deforestation, agriculture and land-use change.
Scenarios include higher temperature, changed precipitation and higher atmospheric CO2.
The greenhouse effect is described as a natural process that helps maintain a warm Earth surface.

sections.heading: Agricultural pathways
content: Higher CO2 can directly affect crop and weed growth.
CO2-driven climate changes can alter temperature, rainfall and sunshine.
Sea-level rise can inundate farmland and increase salinity of coastal groundwater.
Crop production is weather-dependent, so climate changes can affect productivity.
Elevated CO2 and temperature affect respiration, photosynthesis, growth, reproduction and water use.

sections.heading: GWP values
content: Source gives Global Warming Potential values of CO2 = 1, CH4 = 25 and N2O = 310 for the cited comparison.

topics.title: Climate Variability
topics.definition: Climate variability refers to temporal changes in weather phenomena associated with atmospheric circulation and natural or human-related drivers.

sections.heading: Meaning and impacts
content: Occurs from year to year and across regions.
Recurring drought and desertification threaten land-dependent livelihoods.
Weather-related disasters include droughts, floods, ice storms, dust storms, landslides, lightning-associated storms and forest fires.

sections.heading: External causes
content: Solar output changes.
Earth orbital eccentricity varies from nearly circular to more elliptical.
Precession causes wobble of Earth's axis.
Earth's axial tilt is given as varying between 21.8° and 24.4°.

sections.heading: Internal and anthropogenic causes
content: Changes in atmospheric greenhouse-gas composition.
Land-surface changes including afforestation and deforestation.
Southern Oscillation/El Niño–La Niña dynamics involving western tropical Pacific sea-surface temperature.
Anthropogenic greenhouse gases and aerosols.

topics.title: El Niño, La Niña and Climate Variability
topics.definition: El Niño and La Niña are natural short-term climate fluctuations associated with tropical Pacific Ocean conditions and the Southern Oscillation.

sections.heading: ENSO effects
content: El Niño is associated with tropical Pacific warming.
La Niña is associated with tropical Pacific cooling.
Strong events can produce year-to-year changes in temperature and rainfall in many regions.
The source links strong events with extreme weather such as flooding and drought.
These short-term fluctuations are described as smaller than the long-term 20th-century warming trend.

sections.heading: Related drivers
content: Southern Oscillation Index is described through normalized pressure differences between Tahiti and Darwin.
Natural variability can also arise from volcanic aerosols and changes in Earth's orbit.

topics.title: Effects of Climate Change on Agriculture
topics.definition: Climate change affects crop production through changes in temperature, rainfall, atmospheric CO2 and related biological processes.

sections.heading: Major effects
content: Higher greenhouse-gas concentrations are expected to increase Earth's temperature.
Changes in weather can alter crop production and productivity.
Elevated CO2 and temperature affect photosynthesis, respiration, growth, reproduction and water use.
CO2 effects can differ with latitude and environmental context.

sections.heading: Evidence in model simulations
content: The source describes simulations using only natural factors as showing negligible warming or slight cooling over the 20th century.
Including greenhouse-gas emissions and other human activities produced temperature changes closer to observations in the source discussion.

topics.title: Climate Change Mitigation and Adaptation in Agriculture
topics.definition: Agricultural adaptation combines weather services, resilient crops, improved water and nutrient management, and risk-reduction practices.

sections.heading: Adaptation measures
content: Provide value-added weather services to help farmers manage current climate risks.
Shift planting dates when appropriate.
Choose varieties with different growth durations.
Modify crop rotations.
Establish early-warning systems for pest and disease outbreaks.
Use integrated pest management under changing climatic conditions.
Use participatory and formal breeding for heat-, drought- and salinity-tolerant varieties.
Develop short-duration varieties that mature before peak heat.
Select genotypes with higher per-day yield potential to offset heat-related shortening of growth periods.

sections.heading: Drought prevention
content: Use on-farm reservoirs in medium lands.
Grow pulses and oilseeds instead of rice in uplands where suitable.
Use ridge-and-furrow systems in cotton.
Use intercrops instead of pure crops in uplands.
Use land grading and leveling.
Stabilize bunds with stone and grasses.
Use graded line bunds and contour trenches for runoff collection.
Use conservation furrows, mulching and more FYM.

sections.heading: Efficient water and fertilizer use
content: Use frequent but shallow irrigation where appropriate.
Use drip and sprinkler irrigation for high-value crops.
Irrigate at critical crop stages.
Use optimum fertilizer doses and split nitrogen/potassium applications.
Use deep fertilizer placement.
Use neem, karanja and other nitrification inhibitors.
Use lime in acid soils.
Use micronutrients such as zinc where needed.
